How do you initialize a Terraform projec: `terraform init` downloads the provider plugins declared in `required_providers` and sets up the backend for state - it's required before `validate` because validate needs the actual provider schema (what arguments/attributes each resource type supports) to check your configuration against, and that schema only becomes available locally once the provider plugin has been downloaded.
How do you validate a Terraform configur: `terraform validate` checks configuration syntax and internal consistency - HCL syntax errors, missing required arguments, referencing an undeclared variable/resource, and type mismatches against the provider's schema. It does not check against real infrastructure or cloud API credentials at all - a config can pass `validate` and still fail at `apply` time due to real-world issues like insufficient permissions or a naming conflict.
How would you identify and fix syntax er: Run `terraform fmt` first (auto-fixes formatting and often surfaces structural issues) and `terraform validate` to get the exact error message and line reference - HCL error messages are usually specific (unclosed block, wrong argument name, type mismatch), so fixing is typically a matter of correcting exactly what the error points to rather than broad guessing.
How do you configure a Docker provider i: Declare it in `required_providers` (source `kreuzwerker/docker`, a version constraint) and add a `provider "docker" {}` block - by default it connects to the local Docker daemon via the standard socket, or you can point it at a remote Docker host via the `host` argument if managing containers on a different machine.
How do you reference one Terraform resou: Use the resource's type and name to access its exported attributes, e.g. `docker_image.nginx.image_id` or `google_compute_network.main.id` - this both supplies the needed value and creates an implicit dependency, so Terraform automatically creates the referenced resource first before creating the resource that depends on it.
How do you use the image_id attribute of:
image = docker_image.nginx.image_id
Referencing `image_id` (rather than hardcoding the image name as a string) ties the container directly to the specific image resource Terraform pulled, ensuring correct ordering (image pulled before container creation) and that the container is recreated if the image resource itself changes.
Differentiate between terraform init, te: `init` sets up the working directory - downloads providers/modules, configures the backend - and must run first. `validate` checks configuration syntax and internal consistency without touching real infrastructure or needing valid cloud credentials. `apply` actually creates/updates/destroys real infrastructure to match the configuration, after computing (or accepting a supplied) plan.
How do provider version constraints work: `~> 3.0.1` allows any version greater than or equal to 3.0.1 but less than 3.1.0 (pessimistic constraint operator - locks the rightmost specified version segment, allowing patch-level updates only). `~> 3.0` (one fewer segment) would allow any 3.x version but not 4.0 - the number of version segments specified determines how much flexibility is allowed for automatic upgrades.
How would you identify missing Terraform: Run `terraform validate` and read the specific error - it names exactly which required argument is missing or which reference is undefined (e.g. 'Missing required argument' or 'Reference to undeclared resource'), so the fix is directly indicated by the error message rather than needing to guess.
What is the purpose of the Docker provid: It lets Terraform manage Docker resources (images, containers, networks, volumes) declaratively as part of infrastructure-as-code, the same way it manages cloud resources - useful for local development environments, CI test fixtures, or simple single-host container deployments managed alongside other Terraform-managed infrastructure.
Why do we expose ports for a Docker cont: By default, a container's network is isolated from the host - exposing/publishing a port creates an explicit forwarding rule so traffic sent to a port on the host (or, in the Docker provider's case, declared as `external`) reaches the service listening on the corresponding port inside the container, which is what makes a containerized service actually reachable from outside.
What is the difference between internal: The internal port is what the application inside the container actually listens on (e.g. nginx listening on 80). The external port is what's exposed on the host machine for clients to connect to - they can differ (external 8000 mapping to internal 80), letting you present a different port externally than whatever the application happens to use internally.
What happens if the required provider ve: `terraform init` fails with an error stating no available provider version satisfies the constraint (or, if a lock file exists and locks an incompatible version, a version mismatch error) - Terraform will not silently use an incompatible version; it fails fast at init time rather than allowing an ambiguous or broken provider version through to plan/apply.
Explain when you would use terraform ini: `init` first, whenever starting fresh or after changing providers/modules. `fmt` and `validate` during development, to catch formatting and structural errors early/cheaply. `plan` before every apply, to review exactly what will change. `apply` to actually make the change. `destroy` only when deliberately tearing down all Terraform-managed resources in that configuration/workspace - each command has a distinct, non-overlapping role in the workflow.
Why do we use Terraform?: Terraform lets infrastructure be defined declaratively as version-controlled code rather than manually clicked together or scripted imperatively - giving reproducibility (the same config produces the same infrastructure every time), a reviewable change history (via Git), a preview of changes before they're applied (`plan`), and multi-cloud/multi-provider support through one consistent workflow and language (HCL).
What are providers in Terraform?: Plugins that implement the actual integration between Terraform and a specific platform (GCP, AWS, Docker, Kubernetes, Datadog) - they define the available resource/data source types for that platform and translate Terraform's generic operations into real API calls to create/read/update/delete objects on that platform.
What are resources in Terraform?: A `resource` block declares a real object Terraform should create and manage - its type (e.g. `docker_container`), a local name for referencing it elsewhere in configuration, and its configuration arguments. Terraform tracks the resource's state and reconciles the real object to match the resource block on every apply.
What is the Terraform state file?: A file (JSON, typically `terraform.tfstate`) mapping your configuration's resources to their real-world counterparts and last-known attribute values - it's what lets Terraform compute an accurate plan without re-querying every attribute from the provider on every run, and should be stored in a remote backend with locking for any team environment rather than kept locally.
What is the purpose of required_provider: It declares which providers a configuration needs, their source (registry namespace), and acceptable version constraints - `terraform init` reads this block to know exactly which provider plugins to download, and Terraform enforces that any locked/installed provider version satisfies the stated constraint.
Explain resource dependencies in Terrafo: Terraform automatically infers dependencies when one resource's argument references another resource's attribute (e.g. `image = docker_image.nginx.image_id`), ensuring the referenced resource is created first - for cases with no direct attribute reference but still a required ordering, `depends_on` can be added explicitly to force that ordering.
What is the difference between terraform: `validate` only checks configuration syntax and internal consistency (missing arguments, type mismatches) without contacting the provider's real API or needing valid credentials. `plan` actually communicates with the provider to compare current real infrastructure state against desired configuration and shows the exact create/update/destroy actions that would result - validate is a much cheaper, faster, offline-capable check than plan.
How do you pin a provider version?: In the `required_providers` block, set `version = "3.2.0"` for an exact pin, or a constraint operator like `~> 3.2` to allow only compatible minor/patch updates - combined with committing the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file (generated by `init`) to version control, which records the exact resolved version so every team member and CI run uses the identical provider version.
How would you deploy a Docker container: Define a `docker_image` resource for the image and a `docker_container` resource referencing that image's `image_id`, specifying the container's ports/environment/volumes as needed, then run `terraform init` (to download the Docker provider) followed by `terraform apply` - Terraform pulls the image and starts the container, tracking both in state for future updates or `destroy`.
